reason: This passage from Nehemiah 2 describes a social hierarchy where the Persian king holds authority over Nehemiah and others, but it does not claim that the elite are inherently better. Instead, the text emphasizes that (1) Nehemiah, though a court official, derives his ability to accomplish his mission from 'the good hand of my God' rather than from elite status; (2) the common people of Jerusalem are capable of unified, purposeful action when mobilized by shared devotion to God and collective purpose; (3) the actual opposition comes from mockers who scorn the builders, suggesting the opponents' false sense of superiority rather than justified elite superiority; and (4) moral and spiritual authority are attributed to God's will and faithfulness, not to social rank. The text demonstrates functional hierarchy but not inherent superiority of the elite.
